questions.stem: The least common multiple of 8, 12, and a third number is 120. Which of the following could be the third number?
questions.subject: math
questions.explanation: 120 = 2³ × 3 × 5. Together, 8 and 12 only give 2³ × 3 = 24, so the third number has to bring the factor 5 without adding anything that 120 doesn't have. 15 = 3 × 5 works. 16, 24, 32 and 48 have no factor of 5, so their LCM with 8 and 12 can't be 120.

questions.stem: It takes 28 minutes for a certain bacteria population to double. If there are 5,241,763 bacteria in this population at 1:00 p.m., which of the following is closest to the number of bacteria in millions at 2:30 p.m. on the same day?
questions.subject: math
questions.explanation: From 1:00 to 2:30 is 90 minutes, a little more than three 28-minute doubling periods (84 minutes). About 5 million doubled three times: 5 → 10 → 20 → 40 million, and a bit more by 2:30. Of the choices, 40 million is closest.

questions.stem: The remainder when a number n is divided by 7 is 2. Which of the following is the remainder when 2n + 1 is divided by 7?
questions.subject: math
questions.explanation: Pick an easy example: n = 2 leaves a remainder of 2 when divided by 7. Then 2n + 1 = 5, which leaves a remainder of 5. In general n = 7k + 2, so 2n + 1 = 14k + 5, and 14k is a multiple of 7.

questions.stem: If the digit in the tens place of 37,241 is increased by one and the digit in the thousands place is decreased by one, how has the number been changed?

choices.html: The number has been decreased by 990.
The number has been decreased by 1,000.
The number has been decreased by 1,010.
The number has been increased by 10.
The number has been increased by 1,010.

questions.subject: math
questions.explanation: Tens digit 4 → 5 adds 10. Thousands digit 7 → 6 subtracts 1,000. Net change: +10 − 1,000 = −990. (Check: 37,241 becomes 36,251, which is 990 less.)

questions.stem: In a group of 1,200 adults, there are 300 vegetarians. What is the ratio of nonvegetarians to vegetarians in the group?
questions.subject: math
questions.explanation: There are 1,200 − 300 = 900 nonvegetarians. Nonvegetarians to vegetarians is 900 to 300, which simplifies to 3 to 1. Watch the order: the question asks for nonvegetarians first.

questions.stem: Of the following, which is closest in value to 0.52?
questions.subject: math
questions.explanation: Turn each fraction into a decimal: 1/50 = 0.02, 1/5 = 0.2, 1/4 = 0.25, 1/3 ≈ 0.33, 1/2 = 0.5. The closest to 0.52 is 0.5.

questions.stem: A certain reference file contains approximately one billion facts. About how many millions is that?
questions.subject: math
questions.explanation: 1 billion = 1,000,000,000 and 1 million = 1,000,000. 1,000,000,000 ÷ 1,000,000 = 1,000, so one billion is a thousand millions.

questions.stem: Of the following, which is the closest approximation of a 15 percent tip on a restaurant check of $24.99?
questions.subject: math

questions.stem: There were 90 employees in a company last year. This year the number of employees increased by 10 percent. How many employees are in the company this year?
questions.subject: math
questions.explanation: 10% of 90 is 9, so the company grew by 9 employees: 90 + 9 = 99. Choice A (9) is only the increase, not the new total.

questions.stem: An airplane climbs at a rate of 66.8 feet per minute. It descends at twice the rate that it climbs. Assuming it descends at a constant rate, how many feet will the airplane descend in 30 minutes?
questions.subject: math
questions.explanation: Descending at twice the climbing rate means 2 × 66.8 = 133.6 feet per minute. In 30 minutes: 133.6 × 30 = 4,008 feet. Choice D (2,004) is what it would climb in 30 minutes.

questions.stem: Which of the following is always an odd integer?

choices.html: The product of two odd integers
The product of two consecutive integers
The sum of three even integers
The sum of two odd integers
The sum of three consecutive integers

questions.subject: math
questions.explanation: odd × odd is always odd (for example 3 × 5 = 15). The others fail: two consecutive integers include an even one, so their product is even; even + even + even is even; odd + odd is even; and three consecutive integers can add up to an even number (1 + 2 + 3 = 6).

questions.stem: The ratio of boys to girls to adults at a school party was 6:5:2. There were 78 people at the party. How many of them were adults?
questions.subject: math
questions.explanation: The ratio 6:5:2 has 6 + 5 + 2 = 13 parts. 78 ÷ 13 = 6 people per part. Adults are 2 parts: 2 × 6 = 12.

questions.stem:
Helga’s process of calculating the tip to leave in a restaurant starts with the bill for food and drink.
  • First, she rounds the bill to the nearest ten cents.
  • Then she moves the decimal point in the rounded total one place to the left.
  • Finally, she doubles that amount.
Helga’s process calculates approximately what percent of the original bill?
questions.subject: math
questions.explanation: Moving the decimal point one place to the left divides by 10, which gives 10% of the bill. Doubling that gives 20%. (Rounding to the nearest ten cents barely changes anything.)

questions.stem: The mean distance from Venus to the Sun is 1.08 X 108 kilometers. Which of the following quantities is equal to this distance?
questions.subject: math
questions.explanation: 1.08 × 10⁸ means moving the decimal point 8 places to the right: 1.08 → 108,000,000.

questions.stem: The length of a rectangle is 3 more than its width. If L represents the length, what is an expression for the width?
questions.subject: math
questions.explanation: "Length is 3 more than width" means L = W + 3. Solve for the width: W = L − 3. A common trap is to write L + 3, which reverses the relationship.

questions.stem: If this pattern of dot-figures is continued, how many dots will be in the 100th figure?
questions.subject: math
questions.explanation: The figures have 3, 5, 7, 9 dots, so each one adds 2. Figure n has 2n + 1 dots (check: figure 1 has 2(1) + 1 = 3). Figure 100 has 2(100) + 1 = 201.

questions.stem:
x+2y=17
x−2y=3
The graphs of the two equations shown above intersect at the point (x,y). What is the value of x at the point of intersection?
questions.subject: math
questions.explanation: Add the two equations. The 2y and −2y cancel, leaving 2x = 20, so x = 10. (Then y = 3.5, and 10 + 7 = 17 checks.)

questions.stem: What is the least whole number x for which 2x>11?
questions.subject: math
questions.explanation: 2x > 11 means x > 5.5. The smallest whole number greater than 5.5 is 6. Be careful: 5 doesn't work, because 2 × 5 = 10 is not greater than 11.

questions.stem:
Allen, Bridgitte, Chaz, and Diann each live in a different house on the same side of a street. The houses and their numbers are shown above.
  • Only one of the other three people lives next to Bridgitte.
  • Chaz lives next to Bridgitte and next to Diann.

Which person could live in house number 2?

choices.html: Any of these four people could live in house number 2.

questions.subject: math
questions.explanation: Chaz is next to both Bridgitte and Diann, and Chaz is the only one next to Bridgitte, so Bridgitte must be in an end house. If Bridgitte is in #1: Chaz #2, Diann #3, Allen #4. If Bridgitte is in #4: Chaz #3, Diann #2, Allen #1. So house #2 could be Chaz or Diann.

questions.stem:

The same rule is applied to each number in the pattern above. What is the 6th number in the pattern?
questions.subject: math
questions.explanation: The pattern is the squares of the odd numbers: 1², 3², 5², 7², 9². The 6th number is 11² = 121.

questions.stem: In the equation y = 4x, if the value of x is increased by 2, what is the effect on the value of y?

choices.html: It is 8 more than the original amount.
It is 6 more than the original amount.
It is 2 more than the original amount.
It is 16 times the original amount.
It is 8 times the original amount.

questions.subject: math
questions.explanation: The new y is 4(x + 2) = 4x + 8, which is the original 4x plus 8. Each increase of 1 in x adds 4 to y, so an increase of 2 adds 8.

questions.stem: According to the pattern suggested by the four examples above, how many consecutive odd integers are required to give a sum of 144?
questions.subject: math
questions.explanation: The examples show that the sum of the first n odd numbers is n²: 1 + 3 = 4 = 2², 1 + 3 + 5 = 9 = 3², and so on. 144 = 12², so it takes 12 odd numbers.

questions.stem: At the school carnival, Carmen sold 3 times as many hot dogs as Shawn. The two of them sold 152 hot dogs altogether. How many hot dogs did Carmen sell?
questions.subject: math
questions.explanation: Let Shawn sell s hot dogs. Carmen sold 3s, so s + 3s = 152. Then 4s = 152 and s = 38. Carmen sold 3 × 38 = 114. Choice B (38) is Shawn's total.

questions.stem: The point (4, k) is a solution to the equation 3x + 2y = 12. What is the value of k?
questions.subject: math
questions.explanation: Substitute x = 4: 3(4) + 2k = 12, so 12 + 2k = 12, 2k = 0, and k = 0.

questions.stem: The number of gallons of water, y, in a tank after x hours may be modeled by the linear equation y = 800 - 50x. Which of the following statements about the tank is true?

choices.html: It is filling at a rate of 800 gallons per hour.
It is filling at a rate of 50 gallons per hour.
It is emptying at a rate of 16 gallons per hour.
It is emptying at a rate of 50 gallons per hour.
It is emptying at a rate of 800 gallons per hour.

questions.subject: math
questions.explanation: In y = 800 − 50x, the tank starts with 800 gallons when x = 0, and every hour (x goes up 1) y goes down by 50. So the tank is emptying at 50 gallons per hour. 800 is the starting amount, not the rate.

questions.stem: If a > 0 and b < 0, which of the following must be true?
questions.subject: math
questions.explanation: Subtracting a negative number is the same as adding a positive one, so a − b = a + (a positive) > 0. Check the others with a = 1, b = −5: ab = −5, b − a = −6, a + b = −4. With a = 5, b = −1, a + b = 4, so neither D nor E must be true.

questions.stem:
Archaeologists measure the lengths of certain bones to estimate a dinosaur’s height. When the length t of the tibia, or leg bone, is known, a dinosaur’s height h can be estimated by the following formula, where t and h are in centimeters.
If the length of the tibia of a certain dinosaur is 400 centimeters, what is its estimated height in centimeters?
questions.subject: math
questions.explanation: Substitute t = 400 into h = 73 + 2.5t: 2.5 × 400 = 1,000, and 73 + 1,000 = 1,073 centimeters.

questions.subject: math
questions.explanation: Order of operations: do the division and multiplication first. 15 ÷ 3 = 5 and 4 × 2 = 8. Then add and subtract left to right: 3 + 5 − 8 = 0.

questions.stem: What is the distance between the midpoint of MN and the midpoint of PQ shown above?
questions.subject: math
questions.explanation: Put M at 0 on a number line. Then N is at 20, P at 32 and Q at 48. The midpoint of MN is at 10 and the midpoint of PQ is at 40. 40 − 10 = 30 cm.

questions.stem: What is the diagonal measurement of the TV screen shown in the figure above?
questions.subject: math
questions.explanation: The diagonal is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs 30 and 40. 30² + 40² = 900 + 1,600 = 2,500, and √2,500 = 50 inches. (It's a 3-4-5 triangle scaled up by 10.)

questions.stem: In the five quadrilaterals shown above, the midpoints of the sides have been joined by broken line segments. Which best describes the five dotted figures formed?
questions.subject: math
questions.explanation: Joining the midpoints of the sides of any quadrilateral always makes a parallelogram. Each side of the new figure is parallel to one of the original figure's diagonals. They aren't always rectangles, squares or rhombuses; that depends on the diagonals.

questions.stem: Point O is the center of the circle above. Line segment AC is a diameter of the circle. Line segment BC does not pass through the center of the circle. Which of the following is true?

choices.html: The lengths of <var>AC</var> and <var>BC</var> change, depending on how this piece of paper is turned.

questions.subject: math
questions.explanation: A diameter is the longest segment that joins two points of a circle. BC is a chord that doesn't pass through the center, so it's shorter than the diameter AC.

questions.stem: In the triangle, what is the degree measure of ∠ABC?
questions.subject: math
questions.explanation: An exterior angle of 135° at C means the interior angle at C is 180° − 135° = 45°. The angles of a triangle add to 180°, so ∠ABC = 180° − 25° − 45° = 110°.

questions.stem:
A certain 4-sided figure has the following properties.
  • Only one pair of opposite sides are parallel.
  • Only one pair of opposite sides are equal in length.
  • The parallel sides are not equal in length.
Which of the following must be true about the sides that are equal in length?

choices.html: They are perpendicular to each other.
They are each perpendicular to an adjacent side.
They are equal in length to one of the other two sides.
They are not equal in length to either of the other two sides.

questions.subject: math
questions.explanation: This figure is an isosceles trapezoid. The parallel sides (the bases) are unequal, so the equal pair must be the other two sides. Only one pair of sides is parallel, so those equal sides are not parallel.

questions.stem: The point (3, 7) is a vertex of a triangle. When the triangle is reflected over the y -axis, what are the coordinates of the image of the vertex?
questions.subject: math
questions.explanation: Reflecting over the y-axis flips left and right: (x, y) becomes (−x, y). So (3, 7) becomes (−3, 7).

questions.stem: Mary draws a circle and a square on a piece of paper. What is the greatest possible number of points of intersection between the circle and square?
questions.subject: math
questions.explanation: A straight line can cross a circle in at most 2 points. A square has 4 sides, so the most is 4 × 2 = 8. A circle a little smaller than the square, sharing its center, crosses each side twice.

questions.stem: In the figures above, the radius and height of each right circular cylinder are given. If w, x, and y represent the respective volumes of the cylinders, which of the following statements is true?
questions.subject: math
questions.explanation: Volume of a cylinder = πr²h. w = π(4²)(6) = 96π, x = π(3²)(8) = 72π, y = π(2²)(12) = 48π. So y < x < w.

questions.stem: A rectangular pool 24 feet long, 8 feet wide, and 4 feet deep is filled with water. Water is leaking from the pool at the rate of 0.40 cubic foot per minute. At this rate, how many hours will it take for the water level to drop 1 foot?
questions.subject: math
questions.explanation: Dropping the water 1 foot removes 24 × 8 × 1 = 192 cubic feet. At 0.40 cubic foot per minute, that takes 192 ÷ 0.4 = 480 minutes, and 480 ÷ 60 = 8 hours.

questions.stem:
Carlene told Kyle that a rectangular room measured 16 feet by 12 feet, to the nearest foot. This means that the length could measure between 15.5 feet and 16.5 feet and the width could measure between 11.5 feet and 12.5 feet.
Kyle performed the following calculations.
Of the following intervals, which is the smallest interval that contains all possible values of the area of the room?
questions.subject: math
questions.explanation: The smallest possible area is 15.5 × 11.5 = 178.25 and the largest is 16.5 × 12.5 = 206.25 square feet. The interval has to contain both. 179 to 206 misses both ends; 178 to 207 is the smallest choice that contains them.

questions.stem: A rectangular playground has a perimeter of 390 feet. The width of the playground is 75 feet. What is its length?
questions.subject: math
questions.explanation: Perimeter = 2 × length + 2 × width, so 390 = 2L + 2(75) = 2L + 150. Then 2L = 240 and L = 120 feet.

questions.stem: What is the area of the figure shown above?
questions.subject: math
questions.explanation: This is a right trapezoid. The slanted 5 cm side and the 4 cm height form a right triangle, so its bottom leg is 3 cm (3-4-5). The bottom base is 8 + 3 = 11 cm. Area = ½ × (8 + 11) × 4 = 38 square centimeters.

questions.stem: How many degrees are in the acute angle formed by the hands of the clock in the figure above?
questions.subject: math
questions.explanation: A clock face is 360° split into 12 hour marks, so each mark is 30°. At 10 o'clock the hands point at 10 and 12, which are 2 marks apart: 2 × 30° = 60°.

questions.stem: A certain company keeps a list of 50 employees and their annual salaries. When the salary of the very highly paid president is added to this list, which of the following statistics is most likely to be approximately the same or nearly the same for the original list and the new list?
questions.subject: math
questions.explanation: One huge salary changes the highest salary, the range, the mean and the standard deviation a lot. The median is the middle value, and adding one value at the top moves the middle by at most one position. So the median stays about the same.

questions.stem: In a school fund-raiser, 10 students in class A sold an average (arithmetic mean) of 4 boxes of cookies. In class B, 15 students sold an average of 9 boxes. What was the average number of boxes of cookies sold by the 25 students?
questions.subject: math
questions.explanation: Find the totals first: class A sold 10 × 4 = 40 boxes and class B sold 15 × 9 = 135 boxes. 175 boxes ÷ 25 students = 7. Averaging 4 and 9 to get 6½ is a trap, because the classes are different sizes.

questions.stem: According to the box-and-whisker plot above, three-fourths of the cars made by Company X got fewer than how many miles per gallon?
questions.subject: math
questions.explanation: In a box-and-whisker plot, the right edge of the box is the upper quartile: 75% of the data is below it. The box ends at 33, so three-fourths of the cars got fewer than 33 miles per gallon.

questions.stem: There are 15 girls and 11 boys in a mathematics class. If a student is selected at random to run an errand, what is the probability that a boy will be selected?
questions.subject: math
questions.explanation: There are 15 + 11 = 26 students and 11 of them are boys. P(boy) = 11/26.

questions.stem: From a shipment of 500 batteries, a sample of 25 was selected at random and tested. If 2 batteries in the sample were found to be dead, how many dead batteries would be expected in the entire shipment?
questions.subject: math
questions.explanation: 2 out of 25 dead is the same rate as x out of 500. 500 is 25 × 20, so x = 2 × 20 = 40.

questions.stem: Li's English book weighs 3 pounds, her math book weighs 5 pounds, her history book weighs 4 pounds, and her science book weighs 6 pounds.How many different combinations of one or more books can Li pack in her backpack so that the total weight of the books is 12 pounds or less?
questions.subject: math
questions.explanation: Books weigh 3, 5, 4 and 6 lb. All 4 single books work. All 6 pairs work (the heaviest pair is 5 + 6 = 11). Of the 4 groups of three, only 3 + 5 + 4 = 12 works. All four books weigh 18. Total: 4 + 6 + 1 = 11.

questions.stem:
Last month Bonnie recorded the weights of 11 dogs. Statistics for these weights are given below.
This month, Bonnie weighed the 11 dogs again. The weight of one dog changed from 31 pounds to 27 pounds. The weights of all the other dogs stayed the same.
Which of the following statistics changed from last month to this month?
questions.subject: math
questions.explanation: The dog that changed weighed 31, the minimum, and it got lighter. The maximum, mode (88), quartiles and median all depend on the other dogs, so they don't move. Lowering one value always lowers the mean.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes what happens in the story?

choices.html: A young man visits his aunt and tells her about a recent tragedy.
A young girl amuses her family by telling them scary stories.
A young girl makes up a story and frightens a nervous visitor.
A family plays a trick on a young man from out of town.

questions.subject: reading
questions.explanation: Vera, the niece, invents the tragedy of the open window, and nervous Framton flees in terror when the men walk in. The last line gives her away: “Romance at short notice was her specialty.” A gets the roles wrong—Mrs. Sappleton isn’t Framton’s aunt, and he hears the story rather than telling it.

questions.stem: On page 3, the narrator describes the niece as a "self-possessed young lady." This means the niece is
questions.subject: reading
questions.explanation: To be self-possessed is to be calm and in control of yourself. Vera chats easily with a stranger and keeps a straight face through her invented tale; the one moment her voice “lost its self-possessed note,” it became “falteringly human.” She is imaginative too, but that’s a different trait.

questions.stem: Why does Framton Nuttel visit the countryside?

choices.html: To take a tour of the area
To visit his aunt, Mrs. Sappleton

questions.subject: reading
questions.explanation: Early on, Framton doubts these visits will help “the nerve cure which he was supposed to be undergoing,” and his sister warns that moping will make his “nerves” worse. Meeting her friends is something she arranged once he was going, not the reason he went. And Mrs. Sappleton is Vera’s aunt, not his.

questions.stem: On page 5, the narrator says Framton has the delusion that total strangers are interested in his nervous condition. This means Framton

choices.html: has a common illness related to his nerves
is worried about what people think of him
dreams that he is constantly being watched
has a mistaken idea about how others view him

questions.subject: reading
questions.explanation: A delusion is a false belief. Framton assumes strangers are “hungry for the least detail” of his ailments, but Mrs. Sappleton answers in a voice that “only replaced a yawn at the last moment.” A is tempting because he does have nerve trouble, but the delusion is about other people’s interest, not his illness.

questions.stem: What is the main strategy the author uses in the story?

choices.html: He creates conflict among the important characters.
He adds romance to the relationship between the two main characters.
He withholds information from the reader until the story's conclusion.
He creates suspense by disguising the identity of a character.

questions.subject: reading
questions.explanation: Saki lets you believe Vera’s ghost story right along with Framton, then reveals the truth only in the last line: “Romance at short notice was her specialty.” D is tempting, but no one’s identity is disguised—the three men really are the husband and brothers. What’s hidden is that Vera’s story was false.

questions.stem: According to the introduction, what made Roosevelt's inaugural celebration different from those of the past?

choices.html: A wide range of people were in attendance.
Many politicians were invited to participate.
His inaugural address was longer than that of any other president.
It was the first celebration open to anyone who wanted to attend.

questions.subject: reading
questions.explanation: The introduction calls the celebration “the largest and most diverse of any in memory,” then lists cowboys, American Indians, coal miners, soldiers, and students. Diverse means varied—a wide range of people. It never says the event was the first open to everyone or that the speech set a length record.

questions.stem: On page 3, Roosevelt refers to the perils the nation faced. He means the nation faced
questions.subject: reading
questions.explanation: Perils are dangers. Roosevelt says, “Our forefathers faced certain perils which we have outgrown”—dangers from the nation’s past—and contrasts them with “other perils” the founders couldn’t foresee. Population growth is mentioned nearby, but as a source of problems, not as the perils themselves.

questions.stem: On page 3, Roosevelt describes governing the United States as formidable. He means that governing was
questions.subject: reading
questions.explanation: Formidable means hard and intimidating. Roosevelt says “never before” has anyone tried “so vast and formidable an experiment” as running a whole continent as a democracy. Something never tried before can’t be conventional, and “vast” already covers its size, so “formidable” adds the idea of difficulty.

questions.stem: What is the experiment that Roosevelt describes near the bottom of page 3?

choices.html: The implementation of a democratic form of government on a very large scale
The successful industrialization of a country with a democratic government
The resolution of social problems that come with great wealth and power
The balance between American power and the need for peaceful relations abroad

questions.subject: reading
questions.explanation: Roosevelt names it directly: “administering the affairs of a continent under the forms of a democratic republic”—democracy on a huge scale. He then warns that if it fails, “free self-government throughout the world” will suffer. Industrial growth appears in the same paragraph, but as a change that makes the experiment harder, not the experiment itself.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes Roosevelt's ideas about the relationship between progress and problems?

choices.html: He believes that in the future progress will not lead to problems.
He believes progress solves most problems once thought unsolvable.
He believes a nation cannot have progress without also having problems.
He believes progress can solve only certain types of problems.

questions.subject: reading
questions.explanation: Roosevelt says the nation’s growth “is inevitably accompanied by a like growth in the problems,” and that “Power invariably means both responsibility and danger.” Inevitably and invariably both mean it always happens: progress brings problems with it. B is tempting, but he never says progress solves problems—he says it creates new ones.

questions.stem: Roosevelt most likely refers to Washington and Lincoln at the end of the address in order to

choices.html: praise the speaking styles of previous presidents
suggest that government was more powerful in the past

questions.subject: reading
questions.explanation: The final sentence praises the qualities “which made great the men who founded this republic” under Washington and “preserved this republic” under Lincoln. Roosevelt recalls those past achievements to inspire listeners to show the same courage and devotion now. He says nothing about how those presidents spoke or how powerful government was.

questions.stem: Mary does not criticize Silas' offer to help on the farm the way Warren does because

choices.html: she knows Silas is only attempting to save his self-respect
she believes that Warren really needs his help with haying
she wants Silas to please his brother
she does not want Silas to think she is rude

questions.subject: reading
questions.explanation: Mary tells Warren, “Surely you wouldn’t grudge the poor old man / Some humble way to save his self-respect” (lines 52–53). Offering to ditch the meadow lets Silas come home without admitting he needs charity. She doesn’t think Warren needs the help—she’s sure “His working days are done” (line 160).

questions.stem: Mary meets Warren at the door and tells him that Silas is back so that

choices.html: they can go to the market for some tobacco
Warren can count on Silas' help to ditch the meadow
they can call Silas' brother to pick up Silas
Warren will be careful about what he said

questions.subject: reading
questions.explanation: Mary hurries to meet Warren “with the news / And put him on his guard” (lines 4–5), tells him “Be kind” (line 7), and later hushes him: “not so loud: he’ll hear you” (line 31). She wants Warren to watch his words so Silas isn’t hurt. The “market things” are just groceries she sets down.

questions.stem: What is really bothering Warren about Silas' return?

choices.html: He does not have the money to pay Silas' salary.
He does not like to get in arguments with Silas.
He believes Silas will leave again.
Silas does not work hard enough to suit him.

questions.subject: reading
questions.explanation: Warren’s real complaint is in lines 17–18: “What help he is there’s no depending on. / Off he goes always when I need him most.” Silas leaves at haying time and comes back in winter (lines 29–30). The wages (A) are just part of their old argument; what angers Warren is being left without help.

questions.stem: How did Silas view formal education?

choices.html: He said it was necessary in order to be self-assured.
He valued it as a way to learn farming.
He thought it was impractical and a waste of time.
He felt it caused people to argue too much.

questions.subject: reading
questions.explanation: Silas thought Harold’s doubt that you could find water with a hazel prong “showed how much good school had ever done him” (line 87). He “hates to see a boy the fool of books” (line 101) and wants to teach him something practical instead: how to build a load of hay.

questions.stem: What does Mary mean when she says that home is "Something you somehow haven't to deserve"?

choices.html: You have to work hard to be part of a family.
It is a place where people merely tolerate you.
You do not have to be related to someone to be accepted.
It is something you do not have to earn.

questions.subject: reading
questions.explanation: “Haven’t to deserve” is an old way of saying “don’t have to deserve.” Warren calls home the place where “They have to take you in” (line 123); Mary offers a warmer idea—home is something you don’t have to earn. C is tempting since Silas isn’t family, but her point is about deserving, not being related.

questions.subject: reading
questions.stem: In line 3, what do the words “exits” and “entrances” represent in this selection?
questions.explanation: Jacques compares the world to a stage and people to actors. An actor enters to begin a part and exits at the end, so a person’s entrance is birth and exit is death. The speech then traces one life from “the infant” (line 5) to “mere oblivion” (line 27).

questions.subject: reading
questions.stem: How does Shakespeare characterize a soldier in lines 11–15?

choices.html: A soldier is short-tempered and eager for fame.
A soldier is loving and faithful to his mistress.
A soldier is honorable and loyal to the throne.
A soldier is jealous and cowardly in battle.

questions.explanation: The soldier is “sudden and quick in quarrel” (line 13)—short-tempered—and seeks “the bubble reputation / Even in the cannon’s mouth” (lines 14–15), chasing fame even into deadly danger. D is a trap: he is “Jealous in honour,” but walking into the cannon’s mouth is the opposite of cowardly.

questions.subject: reading
questions.stem: In lines 23–25, what does Shakespeare most likely mean by “his big manly voice, / Turning again toward childish treble, pipes / And whistles in his sound”?

choices.html: The aging man plays many musical instruments.
The aging man’s voice changes from deep to high.
The aging man snores loudly in his sleep.
The aging man sings playful songs to his grandchildren.

questions.explanation: Treble is a high-pitched voice, like a child’s. As the old man ages, his once-deep voice turns thin and high, so it “pipes / And whistles” like a reed or a whistle. The musical words describe how his voice sounds, not instruments he plays, and nothing here mentions sleep or grandchildren.

questions.subject: reading
questions.stem: In line 27, the word oblivion most likely means
questions.explanation: Oblivion is total nothingness or forgetting. Line 28 spells it out: “Sans teeth, sans eyes, sans taste, sans everything,” and sans means “without,” so being without everything is nothingness. Misery may sound fitting for old age, but these lines describe absence, not suffering.

questions.subject: reading
questions.stem: The author conveys the mood of this chapter by focusing mainly on
questions.explanation: Almost the whole chapter describes the place: the “gloomy” prison front, the rusty “ponderous iron-work,” the “unsightly vegetation,” the wild rose-bush. No one speaks, nothing happens, and no character is developed, so the mood comes from setting. Personification shows up only in passing, as in “the deep heart of Nature.”

questions.subject: reading
questions.stem: Which of the following phrases best expresses the main idea of the chapter?

choices.html: Sometimes the dreariest place may contain a ray of hope.
Colonists who do not uphold the law deserve to die.
Virtue is not enough to protect one from death.
Ancient surroundings tend to attract evil-doers.

questions.explanation: Most of the chapter is grim—a prison, a cemetery, weeds. But at the prison door grows a wild rose-bush offering “fragrance and fragile beauty” to prisoners, a sign “that the deep heart of Nature could pity and be kind” (lines 34–37). The narrator even hopes it may “relieve the darkening close” of the tale.

questions.subject: reading
questions.stem: Which of the following is the best context clue to indicate that this is the first chapter of the novel?

choices.html: “whatever Utopia of human virtue and happiness they might originally project”
“the deep heart of Nature could pity and be kind to him”
“the wooden jail was already marked with weather-stains and other indications of age”
“the threshold of our narrative, which is now about to issue from that inauspicious portal”

questions.explanation: Near the end, the narrator speaks of “the threshold of our narrative, which is now about to issue from that inauspicious portal” (lines 45–46). A threshold is a doorway: the story is just stepping out to begin. The other quotes describe the colony, Nature, or the old jail, not where we are in the story.

questions.subject: reading
questions.stem: All of the following words could be used to describe the mood of lines 1–3 except
questions.explanation: “Sad-colored garments” and “gray, steeple-crowned hats” make the scene cheerless, colorless, and grave. Nothing in these lines suggests anyone defying authority—the crowd simply stands assembled in front of the prison. That makes rebellious the one word that doesn’t fit.

questions.subject: reading
questions.stem: According to the chapter, where was the wild rose-bush growing?
questions.explanation: Lines 30–32 place it exactly: “on one side of the portal, and rooted almost at the threshold, was a wild rose-bush.” A portal is a doorway, so the rose grows beside the prison door. The weeds fill the grass-plot between the jail and the street; the word “But” sets the rose apart from them.

questions.subject: reading
questions.stem: What is the best synonym for the word edifice as it is used in line 4?
questions.explanation: An edifice is a large building. In line 4 the crowd stands before “a wooden edifice, the door of which was heavily timbered with oak”—the edifice has a door, so it can’t be the door. It turns out to be the prison, which line 25 calls “this ugly edifice.”

questions.subject: reading
questions.stem:
Read the phrase from lines 26–28 in the box below.
a grass-plot, much overgrown with
burdock, pig-weed, apple-peru, and
such unsightly vegetation
Which of the following words is the best synonym for the word unsightly?
questions.explanation: Unsightly means unpleasant to look at—notice “sight” inside the word. The weeds are set against the rose’s “delicate gems” and “fragile beauty,” so they’re unattractive. Unhealthy is tempting, but these weeds are thriving: they find something “congenial in the soil” (line 29).

questions.subject: reading
questions.stem: What is emphasized in stanzas 1 and 2?

choices.html: reasons for the reader to take action
the importance of reevaluating one’s life

questions.explanation: Both stanzas open with “Life has loveliness to sell” and then list beautiful things: waves, fire, children’s faces, music, rain-wet pines, loving eyes. The call to action—“Spend all you have”—doesn’t come until stanza 3. Children appear as just one example among many, so the last choice is too narrow.

questions.subject: reading
questions.stem: Which of the following figures of speech is used in line 4?
questions.explanation: “Soaring fire that sways and sings” gives fire human actions—swaying and singing—which is personification. There’s no “like” or “as” in line 4, so it isn’t a simile (line 6’s “like a cup” is). And “sings” isn’t a sound-imitating word, so it isn’t onomatopoeia.

questions.subject: reading
questions.stem: What does line 10 suggest to the reader?

choices.html: the surprises one can find in nature

questions.explanation: “Eyes that love you, arms that hold” describes love and a hug—the warmth people give each other. Unlike the waves and pine trees around it, this example of loveliness comes from people, not nature, which rules out surprises in nature. Nothing in the line is aggressive or unpredictable.

questions.subject: reading
questions.stem: Which of the following lines from the poem states that beauty is worth any sacrifice?

choices.html: “For one white singing hour of peace”

questions.explanation: Line 13, “Spend all you have for loveliness,” means pay any price for beauty, even giving up everything you have. Line 14 backs it up: “never count the cost.” The first line only says life offers beauty, and “one white singing hour of peace” names the reward, not the sacrifice.

questions.subject: reading
questions.stem: Which of the following is suggested by the imagery in paragraph 1?
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 keeps returning to sameness: streets “very like one another,” people “equally like one another” who move “at the same hours, with the same sound upon the same pavements, to do the same work.” Even each year is “the counterpart of the last.” Efficiency may suit a factory town, but the imagery stresses monotony.

questions.subject: reading
questions.stem:
Read the sentence from paragraph 1 in the box below.
It was a town of machinery and
tall chimneys, out of which
interminable serpents of smoke
trailed themselves forever and
ever, and never got uncoiled.
What does the serpent metaphor emphasize?

choices.html: the long-term dangers of snakes and machines
the unending poisonous effects of industrialization

questions.explanation: Smoke that trails “forever and ever” and “never got uncoiled” never stops, and serpents suggest something poisonous and menacing. So the metaphor makes factory pollution an endless, harmful presence. The first choice takes the snakes literally, and the chimneys are “tall,” not crooked—it’s the smoke that coils.

questions.subject: reading
questions.stem:
Read the sentence from paragraph 3 in the box below.
The jail might have been the
infirmary, the infirmary might
have been the jail, the townhall
might have been either, or both,
or anything else, for anything
that appeared to the contrary in
the graces of their construction.
What does this sentence mean?

choices.html: Though their purposes vary, the buildings look the same.
The infirmary is between the jail and the townhall.
The citizens of Coketown often confuse the buildings.
With each new construction, Coketown becomes more appealing.

questions.explanation: The jail, the infirmary (a hospital), and the town hall have very different purposes, yet nothing in “the graces of their construction” tells them apart—any one could pass for another. That fits the excerpt’s point about sameness. C goes too far: the sentence is about how the buildings look, not about residents getting confused.

questions.subject: reading
questions.stem: Novels include many different elements of writing. Which of the following best describes the writing in this excerpt?
questions.explanation: Nothing much happens in the excerpt, no one speaks, and no individual character appears. Every paragraph instead describes Coketown—its smoky red-and-black brick, its look-alike streets, its identical buildings—so description is the main element.

questions.subject: reading
questions.stem:
Read the sentence from paragraph 3 in the box below.
Fact, fact, fact, everywhere in the
material aspect of the town; fact, fact,
fact, everywhere in the immaterial.
The author uses repetition and parallelism to

choices.html: suggest that the townspeople admire Coketown.

questions.explanation: Repeating “fact, fact, fact” in two matching halves of the sentence makes the words themselves as monotonous as the town. Dickens is criticizing Coketown, not praising it—he mocks a chapel as “a pious warehouse of red brick”—and his tone stays critical throughout, so nothing changes.

questions.subject: reading
questions.stem: Which of the following phrases from the myth tells the reader that the games have taken place each year for many years?
questions.explanation: A custom is something people do regularly, over and over. “As was their custom” (paragraph 2) tells you the young people get ready for the May-day games every year. “Weeks slipped by unnoticed” only shows how long Siegfried stayed, and the other two phrases describe the seasons.

questions.subject: reading
questions.stem: In the myth, what do the flowers symbolize?
questions.explanation: Flowers belong to spring’s side: the May king’s followers are “decked with evergreens and flowers,” while Old Winter is guilty “of killing the flowers.” After his defeat, a pole is decked with wild flowers and the Queen of May is crowned with violets and buttercups. Decoration is what flowers literally are, not what they symbolize.

questions.subject: reading
questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why the battle in the myth is called a “friendly fray”?

choices.html: Gunther invites Siegfried to take part.
The fighting is not meant to hurt anyone.
People who know one another have gone to war.
Old Winter and the May king know each other well.

questions.explanation: The fight is a game—part of “the sport” the knights were invited to join (paragraph 2). They fight with staves and willow twigs, sentence Winter “in merry sport,” and laugh throughout. Old Winter is just a role someone plays, so the choice about the two knowing each other misses the point.

questions.subject: reading
questions.stem: In the myth, what does the destruction of the wooden likeness of the king symbolize?

choices.html: the battle between Siegfried and Gunther

questions.explanation: Old Winter is defeated, “doomed to a long banishment,” and then his wooden likeness is stoned, blinded, and thrown into the river. Destroying the image acts out winter’s death—hence the title, “The Many Deaths of Winter.” B confuses Winter’s crime, killing the flowers, with what the likeness stands for.

questions.subject: reading
questions.stem: According to the excerpt, what was most important to Mrs. Bennet during the party?
questions.explanation: Mrs. Bennet’s report of the ball is all about Jane: “Jane was so admired,” and Bingley “actually danced with her twice” (paragraph 12). Even her anger at Darcy comes from “his having slighted one of her daughters” (paragraph 2). She gets to the Bingley sisters’ dresses only after she has finished with Jane.

questions.subject: reading
questions.stem: According to the excerpt, which of the following would best describe Mr. Bingley?
questions.explanation: Bingley has “easy, unaffected manners” (paragraph 1), is “lively and unreserved,” and dances every dance (paragraph 2)—the narrator calls these “amiable qualities.” He even tries to find Darcy a partner. “Unreserved” rules out shy, and all that dancing rules out lazy.

questions.subject: reading
questions.stem: In paragraph 1, what does the word report mean?
questions.explanation: Here report means what people were saying. The news of Darcy’s “ten thousand a year” was “in general circulation within five minutes after his entrance”—nothing was written down or researched; it simply spread from guest to guest. That’s gossip.

questions.subject: reading
questions.stem: The narrator notes that Mr. Darcy seems better looking to other guests once they learn he has “ten thousand a year.” What is the narrator poking fun at?
questions.explanation: Darcy’s face never changes, but the guests’ opinion of it does: talk of his income makes him “much handsomer,” and once he seems proud, he suddenly has “a most forbidding, disagreeable countenance.” Austen is mocking judgments that shallow. D is a trap—it’s Darcy’s manners that are poor, not the guests’.

questions.subject: reading
questions.stem: In the excerpt, Mr. Darcy spends most of his time doing which of the following?
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says Darcy “spent the rest of the evening in walking about the room,” and Mrs. Bennet later complains, “He walked here, and he walked there” (paragraph 16). He danced only twice and “declined being introduced” to anyone else. Sitting is what Elizabeth does, not Darcy.

questions.subject: reading
questions.stem: What does Mr. Bingley mean by calling his friend Darcy fastidious in paragraph 6?
questions.explanation: Fastidious means fussy and hard to please. Darcy has just said there’s “not another woman in the room” he could stand to dance with, and Bingley answers that he wouldn’t be so picky “for a kingdom!” B is a trap: “Upon my honour” is just an expression Bingley uses, not what fastidious means.

questions.subject: reading
questions.stem: In paragraph 9, why is the word me italicized?
questions.explanation: Stressing me—“not handsome enough to tempt me”—implies Elizabeth might do for other men but not for someone as important as Darcy. It shows how far above the company he thinks he is. He speaks “coldly,” not angrily, so anger doesn’t fit.

questions.subject: reading
questions.stem: Which word best describes Mrs. Bennet’s tone in paragraph 12?
questions.explanation: Paragraph 12 overflows with exclamations and repetition: “a most delightful evening, a most excellent ball,” “he actually danced with her twice.” She races through Bingley’s partners one by one. She is briefly “vexed” about Miss Lucas, but she’s thrilled overall; the annoyed one is Mr. Bennet, who cuts her off.

questions.subject: reading
questions.stem: Which of the following statements represents the main theme of the poem?

choices.html: Science cannot fully express the wonder of the world.
Nature is one’s best source of recreation.
Technology causes more problems than it solves.
Learning causes one to become ill and fatigued.

questions.explanation: The speaker sits through “proofs,” “figures,” and “charts and diagrams,” grows “tired and sick,” and then finds what he needs looking up “in perfect silence at the stars.” Measuring the stars can’t match the wonder of seeing them. B is close, but the poem is about wonder, not recreation, and D is far too literal.

questions.subject: reading
questions.stem: In line 5, what is conveyed by the phrase “tired and sick”?

choices.html: the speaker’s sorrow and loss experienced in his life
a sense of the speaker’s poor health
the speaker’s boredom and disappointment with the lecture

questions.explanation: The speaker grows “tired and sick” while hearing a lecture full of numbers and charts, and the feeling ends as soon as he slips outside. He’s fed up with the lecture, not physically ill. Even “unaccountable” suggests a mood he can’t quite explain, not a disease.

questions.subject: reading
questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the phrase “perfect silence” in the last line of the poem?

choices.html: to explain why he has to leave the lecture room
to convey a sense of loneliness and sorrow
to contrast with the sounds in the lecture room
to highlight the pleasure of science and learning

questions.explanation: The lecture room is full of talk and “much applause” (line 4). The “perfect silence” under the stars sets up a contrast: noise and numbers inside, quiet wonder outside. B misreads the mood—he chose to wander off by himself, and the ending feels peaceful, not lonely.

questions.subject: reading
questions.stem: What do the last three lines of the poem suggest?

choices.html: the importance of personal experience with nature
the dangers of losing track of time
the importance of learning about astronomy
the dangers of wandering off alone

questions.explanation: In lines 6–8 the speaker leaves the lecture, wanders off “by myself” into the “mystical moist night air,” and looks at the stars on his own. The poem values experiencing nature firsthand over hearing it explained. Learning about astronomy is exactly what he walks away from.

questions.subject: reading
questions.stem: Which of the following is the best synonym for the word learn’d as it is used in line 1?
questions.explanation: “Learn’d” is an old spelling of the adjective “learned,” which means highly educated. The astronomer is an expert presenting “proofs” and “figures” to “much applause,” so knowledgeable fits. Remembered is the trap—it reads the word as the past tense of “learn.”

questions.subject: reading
questions.stem: Which sentence best expresses the irony in paragraph 5?

choices.html: The narrator is near a place he had been unable to find.
The narrator is far from those who had once misjudged him.
The narrator is delighted by a situation that sounds unpleasant.
The narrator is appreciated by those he had been too timid to ask for a job.

questions.explanation: In paragraph 5 the narrator feels “the purest gratitude” because his skin has “begun to blister and peel off.” A painful sunburn is something most people would hate, but he loves it because it gives him the weather-beaten look of an old traveler. That gap between the situation and his reaction is the irony.

questions.subject: reading
questions.stem: Which statement best expresses a theme of the passage?

choices.html: Confronting serious challenges can change one’s personal beliefs.
People who defy authority can experience unexpected hardships in life.
Being too boastful about one’s accomplishments can result in embarrassment.
People often find satisfaction even when failing to fulfill their original ambitions.

questions.explanation: Twain never becomes a pilot—his hope “struggled to a reluctant death” (paragraph 3)—and his Amazon plan is half-baked. Yet once the boat sails, he becomes “a new being,” thrilled just to be “a traveler!” (paragraph 4). C is tempting, but his showing off never actually leads to embarrassment in the passage.

questions.subject: reading
questions.stem: What do lines 7–17 most clearly reveal about the speaker?

choices.html: He is desperate to share what the road has taught him.
He is willing to risk leaving the familiar for something greater.
He wonders if he will still be welcome when he returns home.
He fears he will be unable to find the road once he goes away from it.

questions.explanation: The road seems to plead, “Venture not—if you leave me you are lost,” and calls itself “well-beaten,” the safe, familiar path (lines 9–12). The speaker answers, “I am not afraid to leave you, yet I love you” (lines 13–14). He loves what he knows but is ready to go beyond it.

questions.subject: reading
questions.stem: What is the main effect of the speaker’s transition from the phrase “I think” in lines 18–24 to “I will” in lines 43–47 of the poem?

choices.html: It suggests his indecision about what he should do.
It emphasizes his growing commitment to his feelings.
It reinforces his ability to complete the plans that he makes.
It highlights the numerous differences between himself and others.

questions.explanation: In lines 18–24, “I think” introduces hopes and beliefs. By lines 43–47, “I will recruit,” “I will scatter,” and “I will toss” turn those feelings into firm promises, showing his commitment growing. C overstates it: saying “I will” shows determination, not proof that he can carry out his plans.

questions.subject: reading
questions.stem:
Read lines 55–58 in the box.
Now I see the secret of the making of the best / persons, / It is to grow in the open air and to eat and sleep / with the earth.
Based on the poem, which sentence best describes the main idea expressed in the lines?

choices.html: People can only improve themselves if they seek the wisdom of others.
People are most confident in themselves when they achieve independence.
People can discover their inner selves when they immerse themselves in the natural world.
People are happiest when they envision themselves as explorers of the world around them.

questions.explanation: To “grow in the open air” and “eat and sleep with the earth” means living immersed in nature. Throughout the poem, life on the open road helps the speaker discover himself: “I am larger, better than I thought” (line 37). B is tempting since he praises freedom, but these lines credit the earth, not independence.

questions.subject: reading
questions.stem:
Read the sentence from paragraph 2 of “Letters from the Dust Bowl” in the box.
Our recent transition from rain-soaked eastern Kansas with its green pasture, luxuriant foliage, abundance of flowers, and promise of a generous harvest, to the dust-covered desolation of No Man’s Land was a difficult change to crowd into one short day’s travel.
Which word could best replace the word luxuriant in the sentence?
questions.explanation: Luxuriant sits in a list of signs of rich growth—“green pastures,” an “abundance of flowers,” and “a generous harvest”—all set against “dust-covered desolation.” It means growing thickly and richly, so flourishing fits. Mature means fully grown, which misses the idea of lushness.

questions.subject: reading
questions.stem:
Read the sentence from paragraph 2 of “Letters from the Dust Bowl” in the box.
Wearing our shade hats, with handkerchiefs tied over our faces and vaseline in our nostrils, we have been trying to rescue our home from the accumulations of wind-blown dust which penetrates wherever air can go.
Which inference is best supported by the sentence?

choices.html: The dust causes serious discoloration of clothing.
The wind is causing predictable weather patterns.
The dust is uncomfortable and even dangerous to breathe.
The measures taken to combat wind are useful and productive.

questions.explanation: Handkerchiefs over faces and vaseline in nostrils are steps you’d take only if the dust hurt to breathe. Later in paragraph 2 she tries “to avoid inhaling the irritating dust,” and in paragraph 10 it worsens Will’s “bronchial trouble.” Nothing mentions stained clothing, and her efforts are “almost hopeless,” not productive.

paragraphs: "My aunt will be down presently, Mr. Nuttel," said a very self-possessed young lady of fifteen; "in the meantime you must try and put up with me."

Framton Nuttel endeavored to say the correct something which should duly flatter the niece of the moment without unduly discounting the aunt that was to come. Privately he doubted more than ever whether these formal visits on a succession of total strangers would do much towards helping the nerve cure which he was supposed to be undergoing.

"I know how it will be," his sister had said when he was preparing to migrate to this rural retreat; "you will bury yourself down there and not speak to a living soul, and your nerves will be worse than ever from moping. I shall just give you letters of introduction to all the people I know there. Some of them, as far as I can remember, were quite nice."
Framton wondered whether Mrs. Sappleton, the lady to whom he was presenting one of the letters of introduction, came into the nice division.
"Do you know many of the people round here?" asked the niece, when she judged that they had had sufficient silent communion.
"Hardly a soul," said Framton. "My sister was staying here, at the rectory, you know, some four years ago, and she gave me letters of introduction to some of the people here."
He made the last statement in a tone of distinct regret.
"Then you know practically nothing about my aunt?" pursued the self-possessed young lady.

"Only her name and address," admitted the caller. He was wondering whether Mrs. Sappleton was in the married or widowed state. An undefinable something about the room seemed to suggest masculine habitation.
"Her great tragedy happened just three years ago," said the child; "that would be since your sister's time."
"Her tragedy?" asked Framton; somehow in this restful country spot tragedies seemed out of place.
"You may wonder why we keep that window wide open on an October afternoon," said the niece, indicating a large French window that opened onto a lawn.
"It is quite warm for the time of the year," said Framton; "but has that window got anything to do with the tragedy?"

"Out through that window, three years ago to a day, her husband and her two young brothers went off for their day's shooting. They never came back. In crossing the moor to their favorite snipe-shooting ground they were all three engulfed in a treacherous piece of bog. It had been that dreadful wet summer, you know, and places that were safe in other years gave way suddenly without warning. Their bodies were never recovered. That was the dreadful part of it." Here the child's voice lost its self-possessed note and became falteringly human. "Poor aunt always thinks that they will come back someday, they and the little brown spaniel that was lost with them, and walk in at that window just as they used to do. That is why the window is kept open every evening till it is quite dusk. Poor dear aunt, she has often told me how they went out, her husband with his white waterproof coat over his arm, and Ronnie, her youngest brother, singing, 'Bertie, why do you bound?' as he always did to tease her, because she said it got on her nerves. Do you know, sometimes on still, quiet evenings like this, I almost get a creepy feeling that they will all walk in through that window—"
She broke off with a little shudder. It was a relief to Framton when the aunt bustled into the room with a whirl of apologies for being late in making her appearance.
"I hope Vera has been amusing you?" she said.
"She has been very interesting," said Framton.

"I hope you don't mind the open window," said Mrs. Sappleton briskly; "my husband and brothers will be home directly from shooting, and they always come in this way. They've been out for snipe in the marshes today, so they'll make a fine mess over my poor carpets. So like you menfolk, isn't it?"

She rattled on cheerfully about the shooting and the scarcity of birds, and the prospects for duck in the winter. To Framton it was all purely horrible. He made a desperate but only partially successful effort to turn the talk onto a less ghastly topic; he was conscious that his hostess was giving him only a fragment of her attention, and her eyes were constantly straying past him to the open window and the lawn beyond. It was certainly an unfortunate coincidence that he should have paid his visit on this tragic anniversary.

"The doctors agree in ordering me complete rest, an absence of mental excitement, and avoidance of anything in the nature of violent physical exercise," announced Framton, who labored under the tolerably widespread delusion that total strangers and chance acquaintances are hungry for the least detail of one's ailments and infirmities, their cause and cure. "On the matter of diet they are not so much in agreement," he continued.
"No?" said Mrs. Sappleton, in a voice which only replaced a yawn at the last moment. Then she suddenly brightened into alert attention-but not to what Framton was saying.
"Here they are at last!" she cried. "Just in time for tea, and don't they look as if they were muddy up to the eyes!"

Framton shivered slightly and turned towards the niece with a look intended to convey sympathetic comprehension. The child was staring out through the open window with a dazed horror in her eyes. In a chill shock of nameless fear Framton swung round in his seat and looked in the same direction.

In the deepening twilight three figures were walking across the lawn towards the window; they all carried guns under their arms, and one of them was additionally burdened with a white coat hung over his shoulders. A tired brown spaniel kept close at their heels. Noiselessly they neared the house, and then a hoarse young voice chanted out of the dusk: "I said, Bertie, why do you bound?"

Framton grabbed wildly at his stick and hat; the hall door, the gravel drive, and the front gate were dimly noted stages in his headlong retreat. A cyclist coming along the road had to run into the hedge to avoid imminent collision.
"Here we are, my dear," said the bearer of the white mackintosh, coming in through the window; "fairly muddy, but most of it's dry. Who was that who bolted out as we came up?"

"A most extraordinary man, a Mr. Nuttel," said Mrs. Sappleton; "could only talk about his illnesses, and dashed off without a word of goodbye or apology when you arrived. One would think he had seen a ghost."

"I expect it was the spaniel," said the niece calmly; "he told me he had a horror of dogs. He was once hunted into a cemetery somewhere on the banks of the Ganges by a pack of pariah dogs, and had to spend the night in a newly dug grave with the creatures snarling and grinning and foaming just above him. Enough to make anyone lose their nerve."
Romance at short notice was her specialty.
passages.title: The Open Window
passages.author: Saki (H. H. Munro), 1870–1916
passages.credit: "The Open Window" by Saki, first published in 1914. In the public domain.

paragraphs: MY FELLOW CITIZENS, no people on Earth have more cause to be thankful than ours, and this is said reverently, in no spirit of boastfulness in our own strength, but with gratitude to the Giver of Good who has blessed us with the conditions which have enabled us to achieve so large a measure of well-being and of happiness.

To us as a people it has been granted to lay the foundations of our national life in a new continent. We are the heirs of the ages, and yet we have had to pay few of the penalties which in old countries are exacted by the dead hand of a bygone civilization.... Our life has called for the vigor and effort without which the manlier and hardier virtues wither away.

Under such conditions it would be our own fault if we failed; and the success which we have had in the past, the success which we confidently believe the future will bring, should cause in us no feeling of vainglory, but rather a deep and abiding realization of all which life has offered us; a full acknowledgment of the responsibility which is ours; and a fixed determination to show that under a free government a mighty people can thrive best, alike as regards the things of the body and the things of the soul.

Much has been given us, and much will rightfully be expected from us. We have duties to others and duties to ourselves; and we can shirk neither. We have become a great nation, forced by the fact of its greatness into relations with the other nations of the Earth, and we must behave as beseems a people with such responsibilities.

Toward all other nations, large and small, our attitude must be one of cordial and sincere friendship. We must show not only in our words, but in our deeds, that we are earnestly desirous of securing their goodwill by acting toward them in a spirit of just and generous recognition of all their rights.

But justice and generosity in a nation, as in an individual, count most when shown not by the weak but by the strong. While ever careful to refrain from wrongdoing others, we must be no less insistent that we are not wronged ourselves. We wish peace, but we wish the peace of justice, the peace of righteousness. We wish it because we think it is right and not because we are afraid. No weak nation that acts manfully and justly should ever have cause to fear us, and no strong power should ever be able to single us out as a subject for insolent aggression.

Our relations with the other powers of the world are important; but still more important are our relations among ourselves. Such growth in wealth, in population, and in power as this nation has seen during the century and a quarter of its national life is inevitably accompanied by a like growth in the problems which are ever before every nation that rises to greatness. Power invariably means both responsibility and danger. Our forefathers faced certain perils which we have outgrown. We now face other perils, the very existence of which it was impossible that they should foresee.

Modern life is both complex and intense, and the tremendous changes wrought by the extraordinary industrial development of the last half century are felt in every fiber of our social and political being. Never before have men tried so vast and formidable an experiment as that of administering the affairs of a continent under the forms of a democratic republic. The conditions which have told for our marvelous material well-being—which have developed to a very high degree our energy, self-reliance, and individual initiative—have also brought the care and anxiety inseparable from the accumulation of great wealth in industrial centers.

Upon the success of our experiment much depends, not only as regards our own welfare, but as regards the welfare of mankind. If we fail, the cause of free self-government throughout the world will rock to its foundations, and therefore our responsibility is heavy, to ourselves, to the world as it is today, and to the generations yet unborn.

There is no good reason why we should fear the future, but there is every reason why we should face it seriously, neither hiding from ourselves the gravity of the problems before us nor fearing to approach these problems with the unbending, unflinching purpose to solve them aright.

Yet, after all, though the problems are new, though the tasks set before us differ from the tasks set before our fathers who founded and preserved this republic, the spirit in which these tasks must be undertaken and these problems faced, if our duty is to be well done, remains essentially unchanged. We know that self-government is difficult. We know that no people needs such high traits of character as that people which seeks to govern its affairs aright through the freely expressed will of the free men who compose it.

But we have faith that we shall not prove false to memories of the men of the mighty past. They did their work, they left us the splendid heritage we now enjoy. We in our turn have an assured confidence that we shall be able to leave this heritage unwasted and enlarged to our children and our children's children.

To do so we must show, not merely in great crises, but in the everyday affairs of life, the qualities of practical intelligence, of courage, of hardihood, and endurance, and above all the power of devotion to a lofty ideal, which made great the men who founded this republic in the days of Washington, which made great the men who preserved this republic in the days of Abraham Lincoln.

passages.title: The Death of the Hired Man
passages.author: Robert Frost
lines: Mary sat musing on the lamp-flame at the table
Waiting for Warren. When she heard his step,
She ran on tip-toe down the darkened passage
To meet him in the doorway with the news
And put him on his guard. "Silas is back."
She pushed him outward with her through the door
And shut it after her. "Be kind," she said.
She took the market things from Warren's arms
And set them on the porch, then drew him down
To sit beside her on the wooden steps.
"When was I ever anything but kind to him?
But I'll not have the fellow back," he said.
"I told him so last haying, didn't I?
'If he left then,' I said, 'that ended it.'
What good is he? Who else will harbour him
At his age for the little he can do?
What help he is there's no depending on.
Off he goes always when I need him most.
'He thinks he ought to earn a little pay,
Enough at least to buy tobacco with,
So he won't have to beg and be beholden.'
'All right,' I say, 'I can't afford to pay
Any fixed wages, though I wish I could.'
'Someone else can.' 'Then someone else will have to.'
I shouldn't mind his bettering himself
If that was what it was. You can be certain,
When he begins like that, there's someone at him
Trying to coax him off with pocket-money,—
In haying time, when any help is scarce.
In winter he comes back to us. I'm done."
"Sh! not so loud: he'll hear you," Mary said.
"I want him to: he'll have to soon or late."
"He's worn out. He's asleep beside the stove.
When I came up from Rowe's I found him here,
Huddled against the barn-door fast asleep,
A miserable sight, and frightening, too—
You needn't smile—I didn't recognise him—
I wasn't looking for him—and he's changed.
Wait till you see."
"Where did you say he'd been?"
"He didn't say. I dragged him to the house,
And gave him tea and tried to make him smoke.
I tried to make him talk about his travels.
Nothing would do: he just kept nodding off."
"What did he say? Did he say anything?"
"But little."
"Anything? Mary, confess
He said he'd come to ditch the meadow for me."
"Warren!"
"But did he? I just want to know."
"Of course he did. What would you have him say?
Surely you wouldn't grudge the poor old man
Some humble way to save his self-respect.
He added, if you really care to know,
He meant to clear the upper pasture, too.
That sounds like something you have heard before?
Warren, I wish you could have heard the way
He jumbled everything. I stopped to look
Two or three times—he made me feel so queer—
To see if he was talking in his sleep.
He ran on Harold Wilson—you remember—
The boy you had in haying four years since.
He's finished school, and teaching in his college.
Silas declares you'll have to get him back.
He says they two will make a team for work:
Between them they will lay this farm as smooth!
The way he mixed that in with other things.
He thinks young Wilson a likely lad, though daft
On education—you know how they fought
All through July under the blazing sun,
Silas up on the cart to build the load,
Harold along beside to pitch it on."
"Yes, I took care to keep well out of earshot."
"Well, those days trouble Silas like a dream.
You wouldn't think they would. How some things linger!
Harold's young college boy's assurance piqued him.
After so many years he still keeps finding
Good arguments he sees he might have used.
I sympathise. I know just how it feels
To think of the right thing to say too late.
Harold's associated in his mind with Latin.
He asked me what I thought of Harold's saying
He studied Latin like the violin
Because he liked it—that an argument!
He said he couldn't make the boy believe
He could find water with a hazel prong—
Which showed how much good school had ever done him.
He wanted to go over that. But most of all
He thinks if he could have another chance
To teach him how to build a load of hay——"
"I know, that's Silas' one accomplishment.
He bundles every forkful in its place,
And tags and numbers it for future reference,
So he can find and easily dislodge it
In the unloading. Silas does that well.
He takes it out in bunches like big birds' nests.
You never see him standing on the hay
He's trying to lift, straining to lift himself."
"He thinks if he could teach him that, he'd be
Some good perhaps to someone in the world.
He hates to see a boy the fool of books.
Poor Silas, so concerned for other folk,
And nothing to look backward to with pride,
And nothing to look forward to with hope,
So now and never any different."
Part of a moon was falling down the west,
Dragging the whole sky with it to the hills.
Its light poured softly in her lap. She saw
And spread her apron to it. She put out her hand
Among the harp-like morning-glory strings,
Taut with the dew from garden bed to eaves,
As if she played unheard the tenderness
That wrought on him beside her in the night.
"Warren," she said, "he has come home to die:
You needn't be afraid he'll leave you this time."
"Home," he mocked gently.
"Yes, what else but home?
It all depends on what you mean by home.
Of course he's nothing to us, any more
Than was the hound that came a stranger to us
Out of the woods, worn out upon the trail."
"Home is the place where, when you have to go there,
They have to take you in."
"I should have called it
Something you somehow haven't to deserve."
Warren leaned out and took a step or two,
Picked up a little stick, and brought it back
And broke it in his hand and tossed it by.
"Silas has better claim on us you think
Than on his brother? Thirteen little miles
As the road winds would bring him to his door.
Silas has walked that far no doubt to-day.
Why didn't he go there? His brother's rich,
A somebody—director in the bank."
"He never told us that."
"We know it though."
"I think his brother ought to help, of course.
I'll see to that if there is need. He ought of right
To take him in, and might be willing to—
He may be better than appearances.
But have some pity on Silas. Do you think
If he'd had any pride in claiming kin
Or anything he looked for from his brother,
He'd keep so still about him all this time?"
"I wonder what's between them."
"I can tell you.
Silas is what he is—we wouldn't mind him—
But just the kind that kinsfolk can't abide.
He never did a thing so very bad.
He don't know why he isn't quite as good
As anyone. He won't be made ashamed
To please his brother, worthless though he is."
"I can't think Si ever hurt anyone."
"No, but he hurt my heart the way he lay
And rolled his old head on that sharp-edged chair-back.
He wouldn't let me put him on the lounge.
You must go in and see what you can do.
I made the bed up for him there to-night.
You'll be surprised at him—how much he's broken.
His working days are done; I'm sure of it."
"I'd not be in a hurry to say that."
"I haven't been. Go, look, see for yourself.
But, Warren, please remember how it is:
He's come to help you ditch the meadow.
He has a plan. You mustn't laugh at him.
He may not speak of it, and then he may.
I'll sit and see if that small sailing cloud
Will hit or miss the moon."
It hit the moon.
Then there were three there, making a dim row,
The moon, the little silver cloud, and she.
Warren returned—too soon, it seemed to her,
Slipped to her side, caught up her hand and waited.
"Warren," she questioned.
"Dead," was all he answered.

lines: Jacques: All the world’s a stage,
And all the men and women merely players;
They have their exits and their entrances,
And one man in his time plays many parts,
His acts being seven ages. At first, the infant,
Mewling and puking in the nurse’s arms.
Then the whining schoolboy, with his satchel
And shining morning face, creeping like snail
Unwillingly to school. And then the lover,
Sighing like furnace, with a woeful ballad
Made to his mistress’ eyebrow. Then a soldier,
Full of strange oaths and bearded like the pard¹,
Jealous in honour, sudden and quick in quarrel,
Seeking the bubble² reputation
Even in the cannon’s mouth. And then the justice,
In fair round belly with good capon³ lined,
With eyes severe and beard of formal cut,
Full of wise saws and modern instances⁴;
And so he plays his part. The sixth age shifts
Into the lean and slippered pantaloon⁵
With spectacles on nose and pouch on side;
His youthful hose, well saved, a world too wide
For his shrunk shank, and his big manly voice,
Turning again toward childish treble, pipes
And whistles in his sound. Last scene of all,
That ends this strange eventful history,
Is second childishness and mere oblivion,
Sans⁶ teeth, sans eyes, sans taste, sans everything.

passages.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
passages.intro: This selection is the first chapter of Nathaniel Hawthorne’s The Scarlet Letter, a tale of a woman and her Puritan community. The story takes place in the Massachusetts Bay Colony in the mid-1600s. Read the chapter below. Use information from the chapter to answer the questions that follow.

lines: A THRONG of bearded men, in sad-colored garments,
and gray, steeple-crowned hats, intermixed with
women, some wearing hoods and others bareheaded, was
assembled in front of a wooden edifice, the door of which
was heavily timbered with oak, and studded with iron
spikes.
The founders of a new colony, whatever Utopia of human
virtue and happiness they might originally project, have
invariably recognized it among their earliest practical
necessities to allot a portion of the virgin soil as a cemetery,
and another portion as the site of a prison. In accordance
with this rule, it may safely be assumed that the forefathers
of Boston had built the first prison-house, somewhere in the
vicinity of Cornhill, almost as seasonably as they marked
out the first burial-ground, on Isaac Johnson’s lot, and round
about his grave, which subsequently became the nucleus of
all the congregated sepulchres¹ in the old churchyard of
King’s Chapel. Certain it is, that, some fifteen or twenty
years after the settlement of the town, the wooden jail was
already marked with weather-stains and other indications of
age, which gave a yet darker aspect to its beetle-browed and
gloomy front. The rust on the ponderous iron-work of its
oaken door looked more antique than anything else in the
New World. Like all that pertains to crime, it seemed never
to have known a youthful era. Before this ugly edifice, and
between it and the wheel-track of the street, was a
grass-plot, much overgrown with burdock,² pig-weed,³
apple-peru, and such unsightly vegetation, which evidently
found something congenial in the soil that had so early
borne the black flower of civilized society, a prison. But, on
one side of the portal, and rooted almost at the threshold, was
a wild rose-bush, covered, in this month of June, with its
delicate gems, which might be imagined to offer their
fragrance and fragile beauty to the prisoner as he went in, and
to the condemned criminal as he came forth to his doom, in
token that the deep heart of Nature could pity and be kind
to him.
This rose-bush, by a strange chance, has been kept alive in
history; but whether it had merely survived out of the stern
old wilderness, so long after the fall of the gigantic pines and
oaks that originally over-shadowed it,—or whether, as there
is fair authority for believing, it had sprung up under the
footsteps of the sainted Anne Hutchinson, as she entered the
prison-door,—we shall not take upon us to determine. Finding
it so directly on the threshold of our narrative, which is now
about to issue from that inauspicious portal, we could hardly
do otherwise than pluck one of its flowers and present it to the
reader. It may serve, let us hope, to symbolize some sweet
moral blossom, that may be found along the track, or relieve
the darkening close of a tale of human frailty and sorrow.
